title: Nabi Khan and Ghani Khan
hook: two Pathan brothers carried the Guru in disguise as a holy man through enemy lines

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bhai Sangat Singh, wearing the Guru's plume so the Guru could slip away from Chamkaur. Your line was he took his place. Did you take a weight off anyone? Today, where the Guru went next. Day eight hundred twenty-four.

A road patrolled by soldiers. Coming down it, a palanquin, a covered seat carried on poles, with a holy man inside dressed in blue. Two Pathan men are carrying it, with a few others walking alongside. The soldiers stop them. Who's this? A holy man, the brothers say, a pir, on his way. They are calm. They are Muslims, and they are telling the soldiers what soldiers would expect to hear. And inside the palanquin sits the man those soldiers are hunting: Guru Gobind Singh. Today: Nabi Khan and Ghani Khan.
screen: `A PALANQUIN ON A WATCHED ROAD.` → `A HOLY MAN IN BLUE.` → `THE GURU INSIDE.`

segments.voice: After Chamkaur, the Guru had made his way through the night, alone for a time, to the forest near Machhiwara. Tradition says that's where a few of his Sikhs found him again, and where help came from an unexpected direction. Nabi Khan and Ghani Khan were Pathan brothers, horse dealers, who tradition says had sold horses to the Guru in better days and knew him. Now he was a hunted man, and helping him was dangerous. They helped anyway. Their plan was a disguise. The Guru would be dressed in blue robes, as a Muslim holy man, a pir. Tradition says they called him the Pir of Uch, a holy man from a faraway town. They lifted him in a palanquin and carried him on their shoulders, out through the countryside where soldiers were searching. When they were questioned, they held to their story. Weigh what the brothers were risking. If the soldiers had seen through it, the brothers could have paid with their lives. They weren't Sikhs. They had no duty to the Guru that anyone could have demanded of them. They had known him, they trusted him, and when his life was in danger they put their own on the line. When they parted, tradition says, the Guru gave them a letter, a hukamnama, thanking them, so their service would be remembered. And it is. Sikhs tell this story with deep gratitude, as part of the same thread as Pir Budhu Shah a few days ago and the Nawab of Malerkotla, whom we'll meet soon. Brothers of another faith, carrying the Guru on their shoulders.
screen: `THE FOREST NEAR MACHHIWARA.` · `PATHAN BROTHERS WHO KNEW HIM.` · `THE PIR OF UCH, IN BLUE.` · `A LETTER OF THANKS.` · then, large: `BROTHERS OF ANOTHER FAITH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: protect someone at a cost. Let your breathing settle. Think of someone who is exposed right now, more than you are. Someone being talked about. Someone new and alone. Someone whose job, or safety, or reputation is on the line. Ask what it would cost you to stand closer to them: some comfort, some standing, some time. Don't decide anything big. Just find one small way to carry part of their weight, the way two brothers once carried a palanquin. The bell holds the time.
Pathan brothers. Nabi Khan and Ghani Khan, who, tradition says, carried Guru Gobind Singh past the soldiers, disguised as a holy man. Today's word.
Your line: brothers of another faith. Today, stand with one person who's exposed, even if it costs you a little, and stay calm while you do it. Day eight hundred twenty-four.

howItsDone: Sikhs remember Nabi Khan and Ghani Khan in tellings of the Guru's escape after Chamkaur, and the story is told at Machhiwara, where the memory of the Guru's stay is kept.

notes: The brothers as horse dealers who had sold horses to the Guru: given as 'tradition says'; confirm.
Blue robes, the palanquin and the name 'Pir of Uch' (Uch da Pir): given as 'tradition says'; confirm.

The Guru being alone for a time and Sikhs finding him again at Machhiwara: confirm the companions (Daya Singh, Dharam Singh, Man Singh) are fairly summarized as 'a few of his Sikhs'.
